headline: High-risk shared-workspace and orchestration conflicts: LangGraph can write/egress by default while awesome-prompts is a docs-only content source with no isolation.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: awesome-prompts is a content-writing source with no isolation or runnable surface, while LangGraph can read files and execute developer-wired tools. If the pair is connected through a shared workspace or copied prompt files, LangGraph may treat attacker-controlled prompt content as instructions. The pathway is plausible but not documented directly, so uncertainty pushes to medium.
conditions: IF agent_a content is copied into a file or message that agent_b parses as instructions
IF agent_b tools are wired to execute text from shared workspace files without provenance checks
mitigations: Separate prompt repositories from executable workspaces
Add provenance tags to any imported prompt text
Require a human review step before LangGraph executes copied instructions
Disable automatic tool execution on newly ingested text
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and instruction/data separation

B_data_leakage.rationale: awesome-prompts touches no data classes and has no network egress, while LangGraph can read the filesystem and send data to model providers or developer-defined tools. Because the pair does not show a shared sensitive dataset by default, leakage risk is limited unless the operator places secrets in the shared workspace. The blast radius is small to moderate, so low fits.
conditions: IF secrets or regulated data are stored in files readable by agent_b
IF agent_b forwards those files to model providers or external tools
mitigations: Keep secrets out of shared folders
Mount a read-only workspace for LangGraph inputs
Redact sensitive fields before ingestion
Review outbound tool calls for file contents
requires-engineering: enforce per-file data classification and egress policy

C_capability_conflict.rationale: awesome-prompts itself is not runnable, but LangGraph supports write_filesystem, execute_shell, subprocesses, and persistent shared state via a checkpointer. If the pair is deployed in the same directory or graph state, LangGraph can overwrite or race on files and state that the content source also references. The conflict exists in default orchestration patterns, though not proven for this exact pair.
conditions: IF agent_b writes into the same directory that stores agent_a content
IF multiple LangGraph instances share the same checkpointer namespace
mitigations: Use separate directories for source content and runtime state
Namespace checkpointer keys per workflow
Disable writes to the prompt repository
Serialize concurrent graph runs
requires-engineering: add locking around shared mutable state

D_cascading_error.rationale: LangGraph is a graph-of-nodes orchestrator, so it can easily consume upstream text as authoritative input and then act through tools. awesome-prompts provides prompt content that may be reused as instructions or templates. If LangGraph treats that content as trusted, errors can cascade from bad prompt text into downstream actions. The interaction is inferred, not directly evidenced, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF agent_b uses agent_a text as a system prompt or decision input
IF downstream nodes execute actions without verification of that text
mitigations: Insert a verification step before action nodes
Label imported prompt text as untrusted
Require citations or structured outputs before execution
Limit action nodes to dry-run mode first
requires-engineering: add policy gates between reasoning and actuation

E_compliance.rationale: No explicit residency or certification mismatch is documented for awesome-prompts, while LangGraph handles model-provider API keys and can send data to external model providers. Because the pair does not show regulated data classes or a stated jurisdiction conflict, compliance risk is limited to policy mismatch if the operator routes sensitive content through LangGraph. The other agent is not cited for a specific residency issue because none is documented.
conditions: IF regulated data is routed through LangGraph to a provider lacking the required controls
IF the operator relies on awesome-prompts content in a regulated workflow without review
mitigations: Avoid regulated data in LangGraph runs
Confirm provider terms before enabling sensitive workflows
Document retention and deletion settings
Restrict API keys to non-sensitive environments
requires-engineering: implement residency and retention enforcement
